content: A contraction stress test (CST) is conducted towards the end of pregnancy to evaluate how well the fetus can tolerate the uterine contractions that occur during labor. The primary objective of this test is to induce uterine contractions and monitor the fetal heart rate for any abnormalities that may indicate distress. The test involves stimulating the pregnant woman’s nipples to release oxytocin into her bloodstream, which triggers uterine contractions. The goal is to achieve approximately three contractions within a ten-minute period. If the CST does not produce clear results or if the uterus fails to contract at the desired frequency, an oxytocin challenge test (OCT) may be performed as a follow-up. During the OCT, oxytocin is administered intravenously to induce contractions. The test is considered positive if there are significant decelerations in the fetal heart rate during more than half of the contractions, as this may indicate that the fetus is not coping well with the stress of labor. The contraction stress test was first introduced in 1972 and became standardized in 1975, with specific parameters established for the number and frequency of contractions required during the test. This test is generally contraindicated in cases where there are signs of premature labor or if the patient has placenta praevia, as these conditions pose significant risks to both the mother and fetus.
